claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys is governed primarily by diminished atomic diffusion kinetics.
Diminished diffusion kinetics are more important to stability than intrinsic mixing entropy.
Diminished diffusion kinetics are more important to stability than surface-segregation effects.
The proposed starting material is a single-phase, near-equiatomic nanoalloy with uniform elemental distribution and controlled mixing enthalpy.
One principal element can be replaced by an element having similar mixing enthalpy but markedly lower diffusivity.
Such a substitution can selectively reduce atomic mobility while leaving configurational entropy approximately constant.
Reduced atomic mobility limits the rate of phase segregation.
Reduced atomic mobility limits the rate of chemical ordering.
Introducing a slower-diffusing species slows elemental diffusion at high temperature.
Inhibiting atom migration decreases local compositional fluctuations.
Inhibiting atom migration decreases phase separation.
Suppressed migration preserves a chemically uniform, single-phase structure during thermal exposure.
The slower-diffusing modified alloy will exhibit less phase segregation than the baseline alloy.
The slower-diffusing modified alloy will retain a more uniform chemical distribution than the baseline alloy.
The slower-diffusing modified alloy will sustain a single-phase structure better than the baseline alloy.
The prediction applies below melting where diffusion is appreciable but not overwhelming.
The prediction is restricted to comparisons in which mixing entropy and enthalpy remain relatively constant.
Surface energy and grain-boundary phenomena may also contribute to high-temperature stability.
A lack of statistically significant reduction in segregation or improvement in structural uniformity in the modified alloy would falsify the proposed dominant-diffusion mechanism.
